body.p: An ESP32 has two Xtensa LX6 cores. JALv3 programs run on the PRO core by default; pragma target enable_cores 2 also releases the APP core at startup, and both cores run the program's cooperative task scheduler. A task can be pinned to one core with a core(...) clause on _task_start.

section.title: Enabling the cores
section.p: The value is the number of cores the program may use. 1 is the default and produces the same image as a build without the pragma. 2 is valid on the ESP32 (PRO + APP); a larger value is a compile error, as is any value above the selected chip's core count (single-core PIC and PIC32 targets have one). The value must be a constant and must appear above the first core(...) clause or _task_core(...) use.

The feature is opt-in and stays that way: enabling it changes the image (startup code, a 4 KB APP-core stack, DPORT setup) and buys nothing for single-core programs. With the pragma absent the generated image is byte-identical to a build without the feature.

section.title: What starts
section.p: At the end of the startup sequence the PRO core writes the APP core's boot address and releases it (DPORT APPCPU reset, run stall, clock, and the RTC stall the ROM holds). The APP core boots into the program's task dispatcher with its own stack. When the program declares no tasks the APP core parks in a self-loop.

section.title: Slots are automatic
section.p: There is no pragma task: the scheduler sizes its slot table from the task ... end task declarations, plus slot 0 for the main program. The -task command line option can pre-size the table; it is not needed in source.

section.title: Tasks are cooperative, and both cores schedule them
section.p: The task model is unchanged: _task_start, _task_yield, _task_suspend, _task_resume, _task_kill and _task_restart behave as on the other targets. With the second core enabled, both cores run the same round-robin over the task slots:

ul.li: slot 0 is the resume slot of the main program. A core with no current task writes its own resume address there when it yields, so main is dispatched like any other task.

section.p: There is no preemption. A task that never yields occupies its core until it yields or ends, and with two cores the other core keeps scheduling.

section.title: Pinning a task to a core
section.codeblock:
_task_start core(2) painter() -- only the APP core runs it _task_start painter() core(1) -- the clause may follow the task _task_start painter() -- any core
var byte c c = 2 _task_start core(c) painter() -- the clause takes a variable too
section.p: Cores are numbered 1 (PRO) and 2 (APP). The clause takes a constant or a variable; a constant is checked at compile time against enable_cores, and 0 means "any core". A runtime value is checked when the statement runs: a value outside 0..N raises the runtime error below and pins the task to any core, so it still runs.

The pin belongs to the task's slot: a plain _task_start clears an old pin, _task_restart keeps it, and a new _task_start sets it again. It takes effect at the next claim, so a running task moves only when it is next dispatched. Core numbering and core are ordinary identifiers everywhere except inside _task_start.

section.title: Reading which core ran a task
section.p: _task_core(name()) returns the core that last claimed the task (1 or 2), or 0 if it has never run. It is an observation for tests and diagnostics; the pin is set only by _task_start.

section.title: The core-range runtime error
section.p: When a runtime core(...) value is outside 0..N, the task runs on any core and the compiler raises the program's runtime error: _error_source = _ERROR_SOURCE_CORE and _core_error = _CORE_ERROR_RANGE. Defining procedure _error_hook() (or including error_hook, which prints [core out of range]) delivers the error at the statement. Like _string_error, _core_error is consume-on-read: reading it clears it, and the hook clears the cells when it returns. Without a hook the cell stays set for polling.

ul.li: Both cores share the same DRAM. Program globals are shared with no per-task visibility, exactly as in a single-core build; two tasks running on different cores can touch the same global, so synchronisation (when it matters) is the program's job.
Each core has its own stack. Task procedure bodies are entered by jump, and task local variables live at fixed DRAM addresses, so a task carries no stack frame of its own across a yield.

_task_yield is only valid inside a task body (using it in a procedure is a compile error): a yield inside a nested call would leave a caller's frame behind while the task moves to another core's stack.
Task locals are allocated statically as on the other 32-bit targets; a task can declare variables.

section.title: Validation status
section.p: The ESP32 suite runs five second-core bodies under QEMU and on silicon:

ul.li: esp32_body_smp_dispatch.jal: a task that never yields consumes the APP core while main resumes on the other core;
esp32_body_smp_affinity_error.jal: an out-of-range runtime pin raises the error through the hook and the task still runs.

section.p: Preemption (timer-driven task switching) is not part of this feature.
